title: Mark 10:32–52
context: Jesus leads the journey toward Jerusalem and gives a detailed prediction of his condemnation, death, and resurrection. James and John respond with a request for honor, prompting instruction about suffering and leadership defined by service. Jesus grounds that instruction in his own mission to give his life as a ransom for many. The healing of Bartimaeus closes the chapter with a contrasting request for mercy and a picture of following Jesus on the way; the traditions share this discipleship emphasis while differing in their wider accounts of divine preparation and the extent of redemption.

verses.text: They were on the way, going up to Jerusalem; and Jesus was going in front of them, and they were amazed; and those who followed were afraid. He again took the twelve, and began to tell them the things that were going to happen to him.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus goes ahead on the road to Jerusalem while those following respond with amazement and fear. Arminian readers see his deliberate willingness to face the suffering he has predicted. Their fear makes the call to follow concrete: faith is not confidence that obedience will always feel safe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize Christ’s purposeful leadership toward the place of his death. He is neither surprised by events nor forced along by his followers’ expectations. Taking the twelve aside again shows patient preparation, as the certainty of God’s saving purpose meets disciples whose understanding remains incomplete.

verses.text: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem. The Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests and the scribes. They will condemn him to death, and will deliver him to the Gentiles.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus names the religious authorities who will condemn him and hand him over to the Gentiles. Arminian readers see clear foreknowledge joined to willing self-giving. Responsibility belongs to the particular actors who participate in the injustice, not to an ethnic group collectively or to later generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the approaching condemnation within the saving purpose Jesus knowingly announces. Human authorities will act unjustly, and divine sovereignty does not make their conduct innocent. His precise teaching strengthens confidence in his mission while excluding any use of the passage to blame a whole people.

verses.text: They will mock him, spit on him, scourge him, and kill him. On the third day he will rise again.”
verses.arminianNotes: The prediction describes humiliation and violence but ends with resurrection on the third day. Arminian readers see the cost of Jesus’ freely embraced mission and the hope that suffering will not have the last word. Following him means hearing both realities rather than selecting only the promise of victory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the risen outcome is as firmly announced as the coming abuse and death. God’s purpose is not defeated by the instruments of human cruelty. Jesus’ knowledge of these events reveals deliberate obedience, while the promised resurrection gives the disciples grounds for hope beyond their fear.

verses.text: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came near to him, saying, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we will ask.”
verses.arminianNotes: James and John ask for a commitment before naming what they want, immediately after Jesus predicts his suffering. Arminian readers see ambition distorting their response to his teaching. Prayer and discipleship must remain open to correction rather than treating Jesus as the guarantor of a privately chosen future.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers notice the contrast between Christ’s self-giving purpose and the brothers’ attempt to secure their own advantage. Close disciples still need their desires transformed. Jesus will expose the request rather than simply endorse it, showing that his grace instructs and corrects as well as welcomes.

verses.text: He said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus asks the brothers to state their desire instead of granting an undefined promise. Arminian readers see an invitation to bring motives into the open where they can be corrected. The same question will later draw from Bartimaeus a plea for sight, sharpening the contrast between ambition and acknowledged need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize Jesus’ patient authority over requests made to him. He does not surrender his mission to the disciples’ wishes but makes them articulate what they seek. The later repetition with Bartimaeus invites readers to compare the brothers’ desire for rank with a beggar’s reliance on mercy.

verses.text: They said to him, “Grant to us that we may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left hand, in your glory.”
verses.arminianNotes: The brothers ask for the places beside Jesus in glory, revealing how they imagine the Kingdom. Arminian readers see the persistence of status-seeking even among committed followers. Mark’s later scene of two men crucified beside Jesus makes their request painfully ironic: they have not understood the road to his glory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the mismatch between the King’s announced suffering and the honor his followers are trying to arrange. The request treats nearness to Christ as an advantage to secure. His answer will redefine participation in his mission before addressing any question of rank or prepared places.

verses.text: But Jesus said to them, “You don’t know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus answers their imagined glory with images of a cup to drink and a baptism to undergo. Arminian readers understand these as the suffering through which his mission will pass. Sharing his path cannot mean simply claiming a privileged seat while avoiding the costly obedience he has repeatedly described.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers connect the cup and overwhelming baptism with Christ’s approaching suffering and death. The cup can also evoke divine judgment borne in his saving mission. The disciples may share suffering for his sake, but that participation must not be confused with duplicating his unique work as the ransom for others.

verses.text: They said to him, “We are able.” Jesus said to them, “You shall indeed drink the cup that I drink, and you shall be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with;
verses.arminianNotes: The brothers confidently say they can share his cup and baptism, and Jesus predicts that they will. Arminian readers distinguish their present overconfidence from the real costly witness ahead; James’s death is reported in Acts 12:2. Their answer should not be treated as mature understanding of everything they have asked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ preparing flawed disciples for genuine participation in suffering, not merely rejecting them because their motives need correction. Their future endurance rests on his care rather than the adequacy of this boast. Sharing his sufferings does not mean adding to the saving sufficiency of his death.

verses.text: but to sit at my right hand and at my left hand is not mine to give, but for whom it has been prepared.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus refuses to distribute places of honor as personal favors and speaks of places already prepared. Arminian readers may relate that preparation to God’s foreknowledge of faithful response, while affirming that honor remains a gift. The verse does not specify the grounds of preparation, so that connection should remain a theological interpretation rather than an explicit statement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers understand the prepared places within God’s sovereign purpose rather than a reward the brothers can negotiate in advance. Jesus’ answer directs them away from competition toward trust in divine appointment. The passage concerns roles and honor in his glory, and should not be made a complete proof of election to salvation.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readers may relate the prepared places to God’s foreknowledge of faithful response, while Reformed readers place them within his sovereign decree. Both affirm divine preparation rather than negotiated privilege, and the verse itself does not state the basis on which these places were prepared.

verses.text: When the ten heard it, they began to be indignant toward James and John.
verses.arminianNotes: The ten become indignant when they hear what James and John have requested. Arminian readers see a community vulnerable to rivalry, not merely two isolated ambitious disciples. The anger does not establish that the others understand servanthood better; all need the corrective teaching Jesus is about to give.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the reaction alongside the earlier dispute over greatness as evidence of a shared need for humility. Resenting another person’s advantage can reproduce the same pride as seeking it. Christ therefore gathers the whole group to reshape their understanding of authority and communal life.

verses.text: Jesus summoned them and said to them, “You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus points to rulers who use authority to dominate others, making ordinary patterns of power the contrast for his teaching. Arminian readers see the need to examine how influence is exercised, not simply who holds office. Disciples are accountable for whether their leadership serves people or secures their own superiority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that Christ’s community must not borrow domination as its model of greatness. The issue is authority exercised for self-exaltation rather than care for others. Jesus will not remove all leadership but radically redefine its character through service and his own approaching self-giving.

verses.text: But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus forbids domination among his followers and defines greatness through service. Arminian readers hear a practical summons to choose the good of others under the enabling work of grace. The saying tests actual conduct, so a title of servant leadership cannot excuse controlling behavior or the pursuit of prestige.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see service as the fitting fruit of belonging to the King who gives himself for others. Authority in the church is accountable to that pattern rather than to worldly success. Grace undermines boasting and turns influence toward the good of the people entrusted to its care.

verses.text: Whoever of you wants to become first among you shall be bondservant of all.
verses.arminianNotes: The language intensifies from servant to bondservant of all, overturning the desire to stand above others. Arminian readers emphasize a willing relinquishment of self-importance for the sake of neighbors. The command addresses the aspiring leader; it does not authorize others to enslave, exploit, or silence vulnerable people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ humbling the ambitions of his followers by making their neighbors’ good central to leadership. Being first cannot be defined by freedom from accountability or immunity from ordinary service. The verse challenges the powerful to descend, not the oppressed to accept abuse as a Christian ideal.

verses.text: For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus’ service reaches its climax in giving his life as a ransom that releases others. Arminian readers understand this saving provision as intended for all, received through faith, rather than limiting its availability by the word many. That wider conclusion belongs to their reading of Scripture as a whole; this verse foregrounds Christ’s costly self-giving.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize a substitutionary ransom that truly secures redemption rather than merely providing an example of sacrifice. Particular-redemption readings connect the many with the people Christ effectively saves. Reformed accounts differ over universal dimensions of the atonement, so the word many alone should not be made to resolve every question of its extent.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readers affirm a ransom provided for all and received through faith; particular-redemption readings within the Reformed tradition emphasize Christ securing the salvation of his people, while Reformed views on universal aspects of the atonement vary. Both locate redemption in Christ’s self-giving rather than human achievement, and neither position follows from the word many alone.

verses.text: They came to Jericho. As he went out from Jericho with his disciples and a great multitude, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road.
verses.arminianNotes: Near the end of the journey, Mark introduces Bartimaeus as a blind beggar sitting beside the road at Jericho. Arminian readers see another person easily overlooked by a moving crowd. His encounter will show what seeking mercy looks like, contrasting with the disciples’ attempt to secure places of honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers notice a dependent outsider becoming the focus as Jesus approaches Jerusalem with his followers. Bartimaeus has neither wealth to offer nor rank to negotiate. Mark identifies him personally without explaining why his name is preserved, so speculation about his later prominence is unnecessary to the lesson.

verses.text: When he heard that it was Jesus the Nazarene, he began to cry out and say, “Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!”
verses.arminianNotes: On hearing that Jesus is passing, Bartimaeus calls him son of David and asks for mercy. Arminian readers see trust expressed through a concrete appeal rather than a claim of entitlement. The royal title and the humble request belong together: he expects help from the Messiah, not reward for his own importance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that Bartimaeus approaches the Davidic King as someone wholly dependent on compassion. His lack of physical sight contrasts with the perception expressed in his appeal. The story directs attention toward Jesus’ identity and mercy rather than toward any ability the petitioner can offer in exchange.

verses.text: Many rebuked him, that he should be quiet, but he cried out much more, “You son of David, have mercy on me!”
verses.arminianNotes: The crowd tries to silence Bartimaeus, but he persists in asking for mercy. Arminian readers see persevering trust refusing to let social discouragement become the final word. His persistence is not a technique for forcing Jesus’ hand; it expresses his continuing reliance on the one he believes can help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers notice how the crowd can become an obstacle to the very mercy that characterizes Jesus’ mission. Bartimaeus continues because his hope rests in Christ rather than public permission. The scene challenges the community to examine whether its management of access protects its convenience at the expense of needy people.

verses.text: Jesus stood still and said, “Call him.” They called the blind man, saying to him, “Cheer up! Get up. He is calling you!”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus stops and instructs the crowd to call Bartimaeus, turning attempted exclusion into an invitation. Arminian readers see compassion answering persistent appeal and creating an open way to approach. Those who had discouraged him must now help, reminding disciples that their role is to bring people to Jesus rather than obstruct them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the decisive authority of Jesus’ command in changing the situation for the beggar. Hope is not secured by overcoming the crowd’s power alone; Christ personally summons him. This narrative call displays grace without requiring every detail to serve as a technical illustration of effectual calling.

verses.text: He, casting away his cloak, sprang up, and came to Jesus.
verses.arminianNotes: Bartimaeus throws aside his cloak, springs up, and comes to Jesus. Arminian readers see an eager, embodied response to the invitation he has received. His action contrasts with the rich man’s sorrowful withdrawal, but Mark does not say that discarding possessions mechanically produces healing or earns a favorable answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see readiness to approach the one on whom Bartimaeus depends, rather than an effort to supply something that will purchase mercy. The discarded cloak contributes to the picture of urgency. The narrative does not state that it represents every possession he owned, so that detail should not be invented.

verses.text: Jesus asked him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said to him, “Rabboni, that I may see again.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus asks what Bartimaeus wants, and he requests restored sight. Arminian readers compare this direct acknowledgment of need with the brothers’ request for honor when asked the same question. Faith brings a concrete petition to Christ without dictating a program of self-advancement or pretending to have no weakness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the personal attention of Jesus, who lets the beggar voice his request rather than treating him as an anonymous interruption. The contrast with James and John exposes the difference between seeking mercy and seeking status. Christ’s question dignifies dependence while keeping the power to answer with himself.

verses.text: Jesus said to him, “Go your way. Your faith has made you well.” Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus on the way.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus identifies faith as the response through which Bartimaeus receives healing, and the restored man follows him on the road. Arminian readers see trust becoming active discipleship rather than ending at a benefit received. The account encourages reliance on Christ without promising that every faithful person will receive immediate physical healing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers distinguish faith as the receiving instrument from Christ as the source of the cure. The immediate restoration displays his effective mercy, while following on the way gives the story a discipleship conclusion. Bartimaeus now joins the journey toward Jerusalem, where Jesus’ service will reach its saving climax.
